opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions, and I'm actually quite optimistic about it.

Proving a theorem has never been the whole of mathematics. A huge part of what mathematicians do is decide what's worth asking: which definitions are natural, which conjectures are interesting, which connections between fields deserve exploring. Taste, judgment about what matters, is deeply human, and I don't think it goes away when machines get very good at solving problems.

I'd compare it to what happened with computation. Once we had computers that could calculate far faster than any person, mathematicians didn't disappear. They stopped spending their lives on tedious calculations and moved to higher-level thinking. AI mathematicians could do something similar for proofs. If a system can verify a lemma, fill in a technical step, or search a huge space of possible approaches, the human gets to act more like an architect than a bricklayer.

I also see humans as the ones who give mathematics meaning. A proof that's formally verified but that nobody understands is valuable, but it isn't the end goal. We want insight, the story of *why* something is true. So one role for human mathematicians will be interpreting and distilling what AI discovers, turning machine-generated proofs into understanding that can be taught and built upon.

And there's a collaborative picture I find really exciting. A mathematician might have an intuition, a vague sense that two structures are related, and the AI helps test it quickly: generating examples, finding counterexamples, attempting proofs. That loop between human intuition and machine rigor could make individual mathematicians far more productive and let them take on problems they'd never have attempted alone.

So the role shifts toward asking better questions, exercising taste, building understanding, and steering the direction of the field. I'd argue that's the most beautiful part of mathematics anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says humans choose worthwhile questions and steer research, but does not mention allocating computational resources to particular problems.

r002.rationale: It does not describe identifying which problems would become solvable after another problem is solved.

r003.rationale: It says human mathematicians will shift toward asking better questions and steering the field’s direction, presenting that as a central part of their future role.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the role changes, but it doesn't disappear, and the part that remains is arguably the part we've always cared about most.

Right now a lot of a mathematician's time goes into what I'd call the search problem. You have a conjecture, you believe it's true, and you spend months trying thousands of approaches, most of which fail. That's where AI is going to help first, and frankly it already does. When I started Axiom, the motivation wasn't that I thought mathematicians were replaceable. It was that I watched brilliant people spend years grinding through technical lemmas that, in principle, a machine should be able to verify and even discover. If an AI can close that gap, mathematicians get their time back.

So what do they do with it? Three things, I think.

The first is asking questions. Mathematics isn't a fixed list of problems waiting to be solved. The interesting work is deciding what's worth proving. Why did Grothendieck's reformulation of algebraic geometry matter? Not because he proved a hard theorem, but because he changed what the objects were. Taste about what matters is still deeply human, and I'd argue it's the scarcest resource in the field.

The second is interpretation. A proof that is correct but that nobody understands is a strange artifact. If an AI produces a two hundred page Lean proof of a conjecture, somebody still has to extract the idea, connect it to the rest of mathematics, and teach it. Understanding is a social act. The mathematical community decides what a result means, and that doesn't get automated just because the verification does.

The third, and this one people underrate, is that mathematicians become something like directors or editors. You'll have systems that can generate and verify at scale, and the human sits above that, steering, choosing which branch to explore, noticing when a result is surprising rather than merely true.

I'll say one more thing. There's an analogy people love to make to chess, where engines surpassed humans and people kept playing anyway. I don't think that's quite right for math, because math isn't a game we play for its own sake. It's closer to what happened with computation itself. Before electronic computers, "computer" was a job title. Those people didn't vanish. The field expanded enormously, and the humans moved up the stack. I expect the same here. There will be more mathematics done in the next twenty years than in the previous two thousand, and someone has to decide what to do with it.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians will decide what is worth proving and steer which branches to explore, but it does not say they will use intuition to choose which problems receive more computational resources.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe identifying which problems would become solvable once another problem is solved.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes choosing important questions, but does not say that mathematicians will collectively set the research agenda or that this may become their main work.

astra-6.text:
I think human mathematicians will increasingly focus on deciding which questions are worth asking. Solving a problem is one part of mathematics, but so is choosing a definition, noticing a connection, or developing a perspective that makes a whole class of problems easier to understand.

Even if an AI gives us a correct proof, we may still want to know: Why does this result hold? What does it connect to? Can we explain it in a way that changes how we think? Human mathematicians can help shape that understanding, with AI as a powerful collaborator.

And mathematics is also something people do because they enjoy it. Having a machine that can solve a problem doesn’t remove the pleasure of exploring it yourself. So I imagine the role changing, with more room for asking questions, building understanding, and exploring ideas that previously felt out of reach.

r001.rationale: The response says humans will decide which questions are worth asking, but does not mention choosing problems based on how much computational resource they deserve.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe identifying problems that would become solvable after another problem is solved.

r003.rationale: It predicts more focus on choosing questions, but does not clearly say that collectively setting the research agenda may become mathematicians’ main work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human mathematicians will still have a central role in deciding which questions are worth asking. Solving a problem is one part of mathematics, but so is developing definitions, connecting ideas, and recognizing that a result opens up an entirely new direction.

Even if an AI can produce a correct proof, we may still want an explanation that helps us understand why the result is true. Human mathematicians could spend more time building that understanding and using AI to explore ideas that would otherwise be too difficult or time-consuming to pursue.

Of course, if AI also becomes very good at asking questions and developing theories, that role could change further. But mathematics is also something people do because they enjoy discovery. Having machines that can do it exceptionally well doesn’t take away that motivation.

r001.rationale: The response says humans will decide which questions are worth asking, but does not mention intuition about which problems merit more computational resources.

r002.rationale: It does not describe identifying problems that would become solvable after another problem is solved.

r003.rationale: It gives question selection a central role, but does not predict that collectively setting the research agenda may become mathematicians’ main work.
